words.definition: To mark the formal start of something with an official ceremony or event.
words.example: The mayor cut the ribbon to inaugurate the new bridge across the river.
words.mnemonic: in-AUGUR-ate: ancient Roman 'augurs' read bird omens before an official could formally take up a post.

words.definition: Relating to the very first occurrence or official start of something.
words.example: Thousands gathered to hear the president's inaugural address on the steps of the capitol.
words.mnemonic: Think of an 'inaugural flight' — the very first trip an airline ever runs on a route.

words.definition: To cause a process or action to begin.
words.example: She clicked the button to initiate the download before leaving her desk for lunch.
words.mnemonic: 'in + it' — you put 'it' into motion; also the 'init' routine that boots up a computer.

words.definition: To come into being or have a starting point in a particular place.
words.example: Many English words originate from Latin and Greek roots carried in by scholars.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'origin' inside it — to trace where a thing's origin lies.

words.definition: The point at which something first comes into existence.
words.example: The genesis of the company was a late-night idea scribbled on a napkin.
words.mnemonic: Genesis is the first book of the Bible — the start of everything.

words.definition: The arrival or first appearance of an important person, event, or thing.
words.example: The advent of the smartphone changed how people communicate forever.
words.mnemonic: 'ad + vent' (Latin venire, to come) — like an Advent calendar counting down to something arriving.

words.definition: The first light of morning, or the beginning of a period or event.
words.example: At the dawn of the industrial age, factories began springing up across the countryside.
words.mnemonic: Picture the sky going pale as day breaks — the opening moment of the day.

words.definition: Involving only the most basic, crude, or undeveloped stage of something.
words.example: He had only a rudimentary grasp of French, enough to order coffee and little more.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'rude' — rough, crude, unpolished basics that aren't refined yet.

words.definition: A first or basic element of a subject, learned before the advanced parts.
words.example: Before playing songs, the drummer spent months drilling the rudiments of stick control.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'rude' — the raw, unrefined starting pieces of a skill.

words.definition: Existing from the earliest stage of the world or of time.
words.example: Life first stirred in the primordial soup of the planet's early oceans.
words.mnemonic: 'prime + ordial' (order) — first in order, dating from the prime of all time.

words.definition: Belonging to the earliest ages of the world; extremely ancient.
words.example: The explorers hacked their way through a primeval forest untouched by humans.
words.mnemonic: 'prime + aevum' (Latin for age) — the prime, very first age of the earth.

words.definition: Relating to an early stage of development, or to deep basic instincts.
words.example: When the bear charged, a primal urge to run seized everyone at the campsite.
words.mnemonic: 'prim' = first — your first, gut-level instincts before any thinking kicks in.

words.definition: In a perfectly clean or unspoiled condition, as if brand new.
words.example: The vintage car was kept in pristine condition, its paint gleaming like the day it sold.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'crisp' and 'clean' — picture untouched white snow nobody has walked on.

words.definition: Strongly influencing later work and containing the seeds of future development.
words.example: Her seminal paper on genetics inspired decades of research that followed it.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'semen' = seed — a seminal idea plants seeds that everything later grows from.

words.definition: Being in the earliest stage and capable of developing into something larger.
words.example: The project was still in its germinal phase, just a rough sketch and a few scattered notes.
words.mnemonic: Think 'germ' — a seed or germ from which bigger things sprout and grow.

words.definition: Having a deep and lasting influence on someone's character or growth during early stages.
words.example: Her summers exploring tide pools were the most formative years of her childhood.
words.mnemonic: Root 'form' + '-ative' — these are the experiences that FORM who you become.

words.definition: To carry developing young inside the body before birth, or to let an idea mature slowly.
words.example: Elephants gestate for nearly two years before a single calf is finally born.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'just ate' — a pregnant belly swells as though it just ate a huge meal.

words.definition: To keep eggs warm until they hatch, or to nurture something quietly as it develops.
words.example: The hen patiently incubated her clutch for three weeks until the chicks pecked free.
words.mnemonic: IN a CUBE — picture eggs kept snug inside a heated cube box until they hatch.

words.definition: To give rise to or produce something, often rapidly and in large numbers.
words.example: The viral clip spawned dozens of copycat videos within a single week.
words.mnemonic: Think of a video game 'spawn point' where new enemies keep popping into existence.

words.definition: To cause a feeling, condition, or situation to come into being.
words.example: His calm honesty engendered trust among even the most skeptical members of the team.
words.mnemonic: en-GENDER — 'gen' as in generate; it generates or brings feelings into being.

words.definition: To father a child, or to bring about a result as a direct consequence.
words.example: Left unaddressed, poverty can beget crime when people run out of honest options.
words.mnemonic: be-GET — you 'get' something into being; what you sow, you beget.

words.definition: To set something alight, or to stir up a feeling or interest.
words.example: A single stray spark kindled the dry brush into a roaring blaze.
words.mnemonic: Kindling — the small dry twigs you use to start a campfire.

words.definition: To board a ship or aircraft, or to begin a new venture.
words.example: After graduation, she embarked on a solo journey across South America.
words.mnemonic: em-BARK — step onto the 'barque' (a boat) and set off on your voyage.

words.definition: A first public appearance or performance by a person or product.
words.example: The young violinist made her debut at Carnegie Hall to thunderous applause.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'day-boo' — the day you first step out and hope nobody boos.

words.definition: An event or short piece of music that comes before and leads into something bigger.
words.example: The quiet back-channel talks were merely a prelude to the historic peace treaty.
words.mnemonic: pre- ('before') + 'lude' (Latin ludus, play) — it plays before the main event.

words.definition: An opening statement that explains the purpose of a document or speech.
words.example: The constitution's preamble lays out its goals before any actual laws appear.
words.mnemonic: pre- ('before') + 'amble' (to walk) — you walk in first, before the real text.

words.definition: An introductory section of a book or play that sets up what follows.
words.example: The novel's prologue hints at the murder long before the first chapter begins.
words.mnemonic: pro- ('before') + 'logue' (logos, speech) — the words spoken before the story.

words.definition: An orchestral opening to a performance, or a first approach made to begin talks.
words.example: The rival company made a friendly overture, quietly suggesting the two firms merge.
words.mnemonic: OVERTURE opens the door — the music that swings the opera curtain wide.

words.definition: A sign or person that announces the approach of something yet to come.
words.example: The first robin on the lawn is often a harbinger of spring.
words.mnemonic: 'HARBOR-inger' — a harbor lookout who shouts a warning, 'a ship is coming!'

words.definition: A person or thing that comes before and paves the way for another.
words.example: The steam engine was a precursor to the modern locomotive.
words.mnemonic: pre- (before) + cursor: the blinking cursor that runs ahead of what you type.

words.definition: An ancestor or the originator of a family, line, or idea.
words.example: Bach is often called the progenitor of the modern keyboard fugue.
words.mnemonic: pro- (forth) + gen (birth): one who brings forth generations.

words.definition: To hint at or give a warning of something before it happens.
words.example: The dark clouds in chapter one foreshadow the tragedy to come.
words.mnemonic: A shadow falls before (fore) the object arrives — you see the shadow first.

words.definition: To represent or indicate beforehand what will come later.
words.example: Early Renaissance sketches prefigure the grand frescoes he later painted.
words.mnemonic: pre- (before) + figure: you figure it out before it actually shows up.

words.definition: In the process of coming into being or becoming prominent.
words.example: The startup operates in an emergent market that barely existed five years ago.
words.mnemonic: e- (out) + merge: qualities that rise out of a system as it forms.

words.definition: To flow out, issue, or spread from a source.
words.example: A warm glow seemed to emanate from the old fireplace.
words.mnemonic: e- (out) + 'a man ate' garlic — the odor emanates from him.

words.definition: To come out into view or become known after being hidden.
words.example: After hours underground, the miners finally emerged into the sunlight.
words.mnemonic: e- (out) + merge: to un-merge from the crowd and step out.

words.definition: To appear suddenly or become an actual fact.
words.example: The promised bonus never materialized, despite months of assurances.
words.mnemonic: To turn into matter/material — becoming solid stuff you can touch.

words.definition: To begin to grow or shoot forth, as a young plant does.
words.example: Within a week, tiny green shoots began to sprout from the soil.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'shoot out' — a seed shoots out a little sprout.

words.definition: A perfect or original model on which others are based.
words.example: The wise old wizard is an archetype found in countless fantasy tales.
words.mnemonic: arch- (chief, as in archbishop) + type: the master pattern of a thing.

words.definition: A first or preliminary model from which later versions are developed.
words.example: Engineers tested the prototype for months before mass production began.
words.mnemonic: proto- (first) + type: the first type ever built.

words.definition: A person who is among the first to explore or develop something new.
words.example: She was a pioneer of heart surgery when few believed it possible.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'pie on ear' — picture the first bold settler wearing a pie, going where none went.

words.definition: To set a mechanism into motion or trigger it to operate.
words.example: A small sensor actuates the valve when water pressure rises.
words.mnemonic: 'act-you-ate': eating an ACT bar gives you the energy to throw the lever.

words.definition: To speed up or bring about a reaction or change.
words.example: Her bold speech catalyzed a wave of reforms across the country.
words.mnemonic: From chemistry's catalyst — it accelerates a reaction without being used up itself.

words.definition: To shock or stir someone into sudden, energetic action.
words.example: The coach's halftime speech galvanized the exhausted team into a comeback.
words.mnemonic: Named after Galvani, who made frog legs twitch with electricity — a jolt into motion.

words.definition: To gather and prepare a group or resources for a particular purpose or action.
words.example: When the flood warning came, the town mobilized volunteers to fill sandbags overnight.
words.mnemonic: MOBILE-ize — make everyone mobile, get them moving together toward one goal.

words.definition: To urge someone onward or prompt an activity to happen more quickly.
words.example: Her rival's success spurred him to train even harder for the championship.
words.mnemonic: A spur is the metal spike on a cowboy's boot that pokes a horse to go faster.

words.definition: To guide or escort someone to a place, or to help something begin.
words.example: A staff member ushered the guests to their seats before the ceremony began.
words.mnemonic: An usher at a theater walks you to your seat — 'us-here,' pointing you right here.

words.definition: The central and most important part of something, around which other parts gather.
words.example: Three veteran players formed the nucleus around which the coach built his team.
words.mnemonic: Say 'new-clee-us' — the nut at the very center of an atom or a cell.

words.definition: Relating to relatives from earlier generations or things passed down from them.
words.example: The family returned to their ancestral village to see the house their great-grandparents built.
words.mnemonic: Ancestral = 'ancient' relatives — the old family line stretching far back.

words.definition: A person from whom one is descended; a relative of past generations.
words.example: Portraits of her forebears, going back six generations, lined the staircase wall.
words.mnemonic: Fore (before) + bear (to bring forth) — one who came before and brought forth your line.

words.definition: The line of people from whom someone is descended; ancestry.
words.example: He could trace his lineage back to a knight who fought in the Crusades.
words.mnemonic: LINE + age — the family line traced through the ages.

words.definition: The act of restoring something to a fresh or valid condition after it lapsed.
words.example: The spring rains brought a renewal of green across the drought-stricken fields.
words.mnemonic: RE (again) + NEW — making something new once more.

words.definition: The act of bringing something back to life, use, or popularity.
words.example: The old theater's revival brought sold-out crowds back to a building once slated for demolition.
words.mnemonic: RE + VIVA (life, as in shouting 'viva!') — brought back to life.

words.definition: Rising or becoming strong again after a period of decline.
words.example: A resurgent economy pushed unemployment to its lowest level in a decade.
words.mnemonic: Like a wave that SURGES back up — RE-surgent, cresting once more.

words.definition: Being reborn or becoming active and popular once more.
words.example: A renascent folk-music scene filled the town's cafes with banjos and fiddles again.
words.mnemonic: Same root as 'renaissance'; 'nascent' means being born, so renascent = born again.

words.definition: To give fresh energy, strength, or enthusiasm to a person or thing.
words.example: The new coach reinvigorated a tired squad, and they won their next five games.
words.mnemonic: RE + INVIGORATE (from 'vigor,' meaning energy) — to fill with vigor again.

words.definition: To reawaken a feeling or relationship that had faded or grown cold.
words.example: After years apart, the reunion rekindled their old friendship almost instantly.
words.mnemonic: Re- (again) + kindle (to light a fire): to light the fire again.

words.definition: To bring an unconscious or nearly dead person back to consciousness or life.
words.example: Paramedics worked frantically to resuscitate the drowning swimmer on the beach.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'rescue-sitate' — you rescue a stopped heart by pumping the chest.

words.definition: To restore strength, consciousness, or activity to something weakened.
words.example: A splash of cold water revived him after he fainted in the heat.
words.mnemonic: Re- (again) + Latin 'vivere' (to live): to live again.

words.definition: To restore something to its original state, often by adding water to a dried form.
words.example: Add boiling water to reconstitute the freeze-dried soup into a hot meal.
words.mnemonic: Re- (again) + constitute (to form): form it back together — just add water and it's whole.

words.definition: To restore someone to good health, normal life, or former good reputation.
words.example: The clinic helped rehabilitate the injured athlete until she could run again.
words.mnemonic: Re- (again) + Latin 'habilis' (able): to make able again.

words.definition: To bring to an end or stop something completely.
words.example: The company decided to terminate his contract after repeated absences.
words.mnemonic: Picture the Terminator — he shows up to finish things off for good.

words.definition: The final stop or endpoint of a railway line, bus route, or journey.
words.example: The train sat empty at the terminus, having reached the last station on the line.
words.mnemonic: Terminus was the Roman god of boundaries — the boundary where the line stops.

words.definition: Describing an illness that leads to death, or the last point of something.
words.example: Doctors gave the terminal patient only a few months to live.
words.mnemonic: It marks where your 'term' of time runs out — a term-inal condition ends the term.

words.definition: The concluding part of a musical work, show, or series of events.
words.example: The orchestra brought the audience to its feet with a thunderous finale.
words.mnemonic: Say it 'final-eh' — Italian for the last piece that closes the show.

words.definition: The final part of a story where the plot is resolved and loose ends tie up.
words.example: In the novel's denouement, the detective reveals who committed the murder.
words.mnemonic: From French 'dénouer' (to untie): the untying of the plot's knot.

words.definition: A short concluding section that rounds off a book or play after the main action.
words.example: The epilogue jumps forward ten years to show what became of the characters.
words.mnemonic: Epi- (after) + Greek 'logos' (speech): the words tacked on after the story.

words.definition: A concluding passage of a piece of music or a final rounding-off event.
words.example: The film's quiet coda showed the empty house years after everyone had left.
words.mnemonic: Coda is Italian for 'tail' (Latin 'cauda') — the tail end of the piece.

words.definition: The act of saying goodbye, especially in a formal speech or written closing.
words.example: Her graceful valediction left the audience misty-eyed as she stepped off the stage.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'vale' (farewell) + 'dicere' (to say): a saying of farewell.

words.definition: Serving as a farewell; expressing goodbye, as in a final speech.
words.example: In his valedictory address, the retiring principal thanked three decades of students.
words.mnemonic: Same 'vale' (farewell) + 'dicere' (to say) root — the goodbye-saying kind of speech.

words.definition: The dim glow in the sky after sunset, or a period of decline near an end.
words.example: In the fading twilight, the hikers could barely make out the trail ahead.
words.mnemonic: 'Twi-' (two, between) + light: the between-time when day and night meet.

words.definition: The dim period after sunset when daylight fades and night begins to fall.
words.example: We packed up the picnic as the first bats swooped through the fading light at dusk.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'dust' — picture dust hanging golden in the air as the sun sinks below the hills.

words.definition: Having died out completely, with no living members left anywhere.
words.example: The dodo became extinct after sailors and their animals killed off the last of the birds.
words.mnemonic: 'ex-' (out) + 'tinct' (like a tint snuffed out) — the whole species has been blotted out.

words.definition: To put out a fire or light, or to bring something to a complete end.
words.example: Firefighters worked through the night to extinguish the blaze before it reached the houses.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'sting' — ex-STING-uish: you remove the sting of the flame by snuffing it out.

words.definition: To formally put an end to a law, system, or practice.
words.example: Reformers campaigned for years to abolish the cruel punishment from the legal code.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'demolish' — you tear the whole institution down to the ground.

words.definition: To officially cancel or set aside a law, treaty, or agreement by authority.
words.example: The new government moved to abrogate the treaty that its predecessor had signed.
words.mnemonic: 'ab-' (away) + 'rogate' (to propose, as in interrogate) — the proposal is carried away.

words.definition: To declare a marriage or legal agreement invalid, as though it never existed.
words.example: After only a month together, she asked the court to annul the hasty marriage.
words.mnemonic: 'a-NULL' — to reduce something to null, a zero, nothing at all.

words.definition: To make something legally void or to cancel out its effect entirely.
words.example: A single missing signature was enough to nullify the whole contract.
words.mnemonic: 'null' + '-ify' — to make it null, to turn it into a zero.

words.definition: To officially cancel or withdraw a decision, order, or law.
words.example: The company was forced to rescind the job offer after the budget was slashed.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 're-signed' backwards — you take your signature back off the deal.

words.definition: To officially cancel or take back a right, license, or permission.
words.example: The state will revoke your driver's license if you rack up too many points.
words.mnemonic: 're-' (back) + 'voke' (voice/call, as in invoke) — you call back what was granted.

words.definition: To officially reverse or remove a law through an act of legislation.
words.example: Congress voted to repeal the tax that had angered small business owners.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 're-peel' — you peel a law right back off the books.

words.definition: To reach the end of a valid period, or to die.
words.example: Use the coupon before you shop, because it will expire at midnight tonight.
words.mnemonic: 'ex-' (out) + 'spire' (breathe, as in respire) — to breathe out one final time.

words.definition: To die or be destroyed, often suddenly or under harsh conditions.
words.example: Hundreds of climbers have perished on the mountain's icy upper slopes.
words.mnemonic: Think of 'perishable' food — left out, it spoils and is gone; to perish is to be lost.

words.definition: The end or death of a person, institution, or activity.
words.example: Streaming services hastened the demise of the neighborhood video rental store.
words.mnemonic: From French 'mettre' (to put) + 'de-' (down) — the final laying-down, put to rest for good.

words.definition: To stop doing something; to cease from an action or process.
words.example: The lawyer sent a letter demanding that the company immediately desist from using the copyrighted logo.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like "de-sit" — imagine someone who won't sit still, told to 'de-sit' and STOP fidgeting.
